title: Israel's First Rescuers
overview: Israel settles among the Canaanites and worships their gods, falls under foreign rule twice, and is rescued by leaders God raises up, most memorably Ehud, who kills the king of Moab.

parts.label: Neighbors left in the land (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: The writer says God left these peoples in Canaan to train a new generation for war and to test whether Israel would keep the laws given through Moses. Instead, Israel married into these peoples and took up their gods.

parts.label: Othniel, the first rescuer (vv. 7-11)
parts.note: Baal was a Canaanite storm and fertility god, and Asherah a goddess often honored with wooden poles; worshiping them leads to eight years under a distant king until God's Spirit empowers Othniel to free Israel. This sets the cycle the book keeps repeating: turning away, oppression, crying out, rescue, and peace.

parts.label: Moab takes control (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: Eglon, king of Moab east of the Jordan, joins with neighboring peoples and seizes the City of Palms, probably the area around Jericho. Israel pays him tribute, a regular payment marking them as his subjects, for eighteen years.

parts.label: Ehud's hidden sword (vv. 15-25)
parts.note: Ehud is left-handed (the Hebrew may mean trained to use his left), so he hides a short sword on his right thigh where no one would check, then kills Eglon alone in his cool upper room. The telling is graphic, and many readers see a mocking tone toward the king, down to the servants waiting outside because they assume he is using the toilet.

parts.label: Battle at the river crossings (vv. 26-30)
parts.note: Ehud escapes, gathers fighters in the hills of Ephraim, and seizes the shallow crossings of the Jordan so the Moabite troops cannot get home. About ten thousand Moabites are killed, and the text reports eighty years of peace.

parts.label: Shamgar (v. 31)
parts.note: Shamgar fights the Philistines with an oxgoad, a long pointed stick for driving oxen. Little is known about him, and because "son of Anath" echoes the name of a Canaanite goddess, scholars are unsure whether he was even an Israelite.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Ehud's deceptive killing of Eglon is presented as something God approved or is simply reported as part of a violent, morally mixed history.
think: When a story celebrates a violent rescue from an oppressor, how do you decide whether the violence was justified?
